section.title: Introduction
section.para: Text can include encoded files: web pages inline images as data: URIs, documents paste base64 payloads, mail wraps MIME bodies, and logs contain PEM envelopes and JSON Web Tokens. The package opennlp.tools.assets finds such assets as exact spans over the original text, identifies their format, and can replace them with text while keeping every offset mapped to the source.

CursorAssetDetector checks encoded prefixes and validates the payload alphabet and padding. Format detection uses up to 24 decoded leading bytes, 36 bytes for JPEG 2000 or encoded PEM candidates, or 45 bytes for EMF candidates. Calendar opening lines and XML root elements use the incremental checks below. Bare runs need at least 32 encoded characters and a recognized file signature. The signature table is derived from Apache Tika's media-type catalog. Recognized PNG and GIF headers also provide image dimensions. A declared media type alone does not provide dimensions. Both dimensions are -1 when either is missing or invalid. PNG dimensions require a leading 13-byte IHDR chunk and positive values no greater than 2,147,483,647. GIF dimensions describe the logical screen. A signature match does not establish that a file is complete, valid, or safe to open. Inferred format names and media types come from the same signature. Formats such as xls and pem-parameters can have several media types.

AU detection uses .snd without restricting the audio encoding. LAS uses LASF without a version filter. AxCrypt uses its 16-byte GUID without checking header blocks or authenticating data. Universal Mach-O detection does not check architecture counts. The shared CAFEBABE signature is reported as class and application/java-vm, not as a 32-bit universal Mach-O file.

Android binary XML detection uses 03 00 08 00, the first four bytes of its XML container header. It reports axml and application/vnd.android.axml without requiring the string pool to be the first chunk. Chunk lengths and XML nodes are not validated. GRIB detection uses the four-byte GRIB identifier and reports grb and application/x-grib without an edition filter. This does not validate message sections or establish support for decoding an edition.

MPX detection accepts MPX, and MPX;, the format identifier followed by a common list separator in the file-creation record. It reports mpx and application/x-project without restricting the producing program. Version, code-page and project records are not validated. Other separators require a supplied media type and do not provide an inferred mpx format name.

Calendar detection requires a BEGIN:VCALENDAR opening line ending in CRLF. It accepts ASCII letter-case variants and unfolds CRLF followed by SPACE or TAB, as specified in RFC 5545. The detector reads this line incrementally, including continuations beyond the usual header probe. It reports ics and text/calendar without checking the version, property order, event data or closing line.

SVG detection requires a root element named svg in the SVG namespace. XML declarations, byte-order marks, comments and namespace prefixes are accepted. The root start tag must fit within the first 64 KiB of decoded data. The XML reader disables DTD processing, external entities and catalog resolution. It stops at the root element; image contents, scripts and links are not validated or executed. A match reports svg and image/svg+xml. When the XML header is too long or its namespace is unavailable without a DTD, callers can supply a media type in a data URI. Recognition does not make an image safe to display.

JPEG 2000 detection requires the 12-byte signature box followed by an ftyp box with complete brand and minor-version fields. Standard and extended box lengths are supported. The primary brand selects format metadata: jp2 gives jp2 and image/jp2, jpx gives jpx and image/jpx, jpm gives jpm and image/jpm, and mjp2 gives mj2 and video/mj2. Unknown brands are not inferred from compatibility-list entries. Minor-version values, compatibility lists, image data and complete file lengths are not validated.

AIFF detection requires FORM at byte 0 and an audio form type at byte 8: AIFF or AIFC. Both use format name aiff and media type audio/x-aiff. The FORM size field does not participate in identification. Other FORM types are not classified as AIFF. Local chunks and audio data are not validated.

PNG, MNG, JNG and HDF5 detection requires the complete 8-byte signature at the start of the payload, including the control bytes. JNG is reported as jng with media type image/x-jng. HDF5 is reported as hdf with media type application/x-hdf. HDF5 signatures after an initial user block are not searched.

Pcapng detection requires a Section Header Block identifier and the byte-order magic at byte 8. Both big-endian and little-endian sections are recognized. These identifiers do not validate block lengths or packet contents.

DEX detection requires the complete 8-byte file magic: dex, a newline, 3 ASCII decimal version digits and a zero byte. It reports dex and application/x-dex. Version numbers are not restricted to a particular Android release. This identifies a possible format, not runtime compatibility or valid bytecode.

DWF detection requires the complete 12-byte header: (DWF Vdd.dd), with ASCII decimal digits at each d. A match reports dwf and model/vnd.dwf. Version numbers are not restricted to particular releases. Drawing records and package contents are not validated. W2D streams and ZIP-based DWFx files are not identified as DWF.

WebVTT detection accepts an optional UTF-8 byte-order mark followed by WEBVTT and TAB, LF, CR, SPACE or the end of the payload, as specified in the WebVTT media-type registration. A match reports vtt and text/vtt. Cue syntax and UTF-8 content are not validated. Bare payloads still require at least 32 encoded characters; an untyped data URI can identify a shorter header.
EMF detection requires the EMR_HEADER type and the EMF signature at byte 40, including the initial space in EMF. A leading type field without that signature is not sufficient.

Timestamped-data detection requires the complete CMS content-type identifier 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.31 at the start of the envelope. BER definite and indefinite sequence lengths are supported, including DER encoding. The identifier must fit within the 24-byte decoded header. A match reports tsd and application/timestamped-data; other CMS identifiers are not timestamped data. Detection does not validate timestamp evidence, signatures or the complete envelope, and does not retrieve external content.

Excel 2-4 detection requires a complete BOF (Beginning of File) record with a supported document type. Worksheets, charts and macro sheets are reported as xls. Excel 3 and 4 workspaces are reported as xlw with media types application/vnd.ms-excel.workspace.3 and application/vnd.ms-excel.workspace.4. Unused BOF fields do not restrict detection. A recognized header does not validate the rest of the file.

XAR archives are reported as xar with media type application/x-xar, not Xara graphics. Encoded XPM images are reported as xpm with media type image/x-xpixmap. OpenEXR headers are reported as exr with media type image/x-exr. The signature does not establish ACES conformance. TIFF and BigTIFF headers are recognized in both byte orders.
DXB detection requires the complete 19-byte header, including the control bytes. Snappy streams are recognized by the stream identifier chunk, not just the sNaPpY text.

Explicitly typed, base64 data: URIs accept non-empty payloads, including one- and two-byte values. The media type retains parameters such as charset=UTF-8; the format name excludes them. Non-base64 data URIs and percent-encoded payload characters are not supported. A media type supplied in the URI overrides the inferred media type without changing a recognized format name. It does not establish that the payload conforms to that type.

Malformed padding, mixed standard and URL-safe alphabets, and line-wrapped URL-safe payloads are rejected. For an unpadded run with length 1 modulo 4, the scanner omits the final character to recover a decodable prefix. This recovery does not repair or validate the underlying file.

section.title: Detecting and decoding
Wrapped base64, PEM, and JWT
section.para: Bare standard-base64 payloads can cross LF or CRLF line separators when their continued lines use the conventional 76-column MIME or 64-column PEM width. The final line may be shorter. Unwrapped payloads may instead use the URL-safe alphabet from RFC 4648 section 5. The detector still requires a known and decoded file magic before it reports either form as a bare asset.

A textual envelope following RFC 7468 is different: its verified, matching BEGIN and END labels identify the content. The asset span covers the full envelope while the payload span covers only its line-wrapped body, so decode returns the DER bytes directly. Empty bodies, mismatched labels, lines longer than 64 characters, invalid padding, and non-base64 body characters fail closed.

section.title: Folding assets into text
section.para:
AssetAnnotator provides the opennlp:assets layer, and AssetFolder replaces every asset with text. The result is an AlignedText: spans over the folded text map back to exact original offsets, so downstream findings over the cleaned text still locate in the raw input. The default replacement renders a caption from the asset's own metadata:
Document document = new AssetAnnotator().annotate(Document.of(text)); AlignedText folded = AssetFolder.fold(document, AssetFolder.caption()); // folded.normalizedString() = "An image [png 5x7, 45 bytes] follows."
Mapping the caption back recovers the asset's exact span in the original: folded.toOriginalSpan(9, 28), the caption's offsets in the folded text, returns the span of the whole data URI.

What replaces an asset is the caller's choice through the replacement function. A BinaryContentDescriber can extract document text or generate an image description:
BinaryContentDescriber describer = ...; // supplied by the caller
AlignedText described = AssetFolder.fold(document, annotation -> describer.describe(annotation.value().decode(text), annotation.value().mediaType()));
The interface takes bytes and a media type and returns text. OpenNLP ships no implementation. Applications provide the extraction or captioning service.
